text:
CHRISTIAN:
  But how did you manage it,
  Since we have been blockaded, to—?...

CYRANO:
  Oh!... before dawn
  I could get through...

CHRISTIAN (folding his arms):
  Ah! So it is still that simple?
  And how many times a week have I written?... Twice?—Three times?—
  Four?—

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Every day?

CYRANO:
  Yes, every day.—Twice.

CHRISTIAN (violently):
  And that intoxicated you, and the intoxication was such
  That you defied death...

CYRANO (seeing Roxane returning):
  Be quiet! Not in front of her!
  (He swiftly goes back into his tent.)



Scene 4.VIII.

Roxane, Christian; in the background, cadets coming and going. Carbon and De
Guiche give orders.


ROXANE (running to Christian):
  And now, Christian!...

CHRISTIAN (taking her hands):
  And now, tell me
  Why, by these frightful roads, why
  Through all these ranks of soldiers and reiters,
  You joined me here?

ROXANE:
  It is because of the letters!

CHRISTIAN:
  What did you say?

ROXANE:
  Too bad for you if I run these risks!
  It is your letters that have intoxicated me! Ah! Think
  How many you have written me for the past month,
  And always more beautiful!

CHRISTIAN:
  What! For a few little
  Love letters...

ROXANE:
  Be quiet! You cannot know!
  My God, I adored you, it is true, ever since one evening,
  In a voice I had not known was yours, beneath my window,
  Your soul began to make itself known...
  Well! Your letters, you see, for the past month,
  Are as though all the while I were hearing it, your voice
  From that evening, so tender, and which enfolds you!
  Too bad for you, I come running. Wise Penelope
  Would not have remained beneath her roof embroidering,
  Had Lord Ulysses written as you do,
  But to join him, as mad as Helen,
  She would have sent her balls of wool packing!...

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I reread, I swooned,
  I was yours. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal flown from your soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Love, powerful, sincere...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  One can feel that, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! How clearly one can feel it!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you have come?...

ROXANE:
  I have come (O my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me up if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, and so it is my soul I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I have come to ask your forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted you by loving you for your beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in horror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight,—
  Your beauty holding me back, your soul drawing me onward,
  I loved you for the two together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! You yourself at last triumph over yourself,
  And it is now for your soul alone that I love you!

CHRISTIAN (stepping back):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for what one is costumed in for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But your dear mind effaces your face,
  And the beauty by which you first pleased me,
  Now I see more clearly... and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Do you still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, you cannot believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until now?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! You understand nothing about it!
  It is now that I love better, that I love well!
  It is what makes you you, do you hear, that I adore!
  And less dazzling...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be quiet!

ROXANE:
  I would still love you!
  If all your beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is your joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (pointing out a group of cadets to her in the background):
  My love took you away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile at them a little, since they are going to die... go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; in the background, Roxane conversing with Carbon and several cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? You are pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is you she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She now loves only my soul!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed you she loves—and you love her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More than that.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told you that!

CHRISTIAN:
  There!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told you that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad the thought occurred to her
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word,
  Come, do not become ugly: she would hold it too much against me!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  You are going to tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  No, no! Not that torment.

CHRISTIAN:
  Would I destroy your happiness because I am handsome?
  It is too unjust!

CYRANO:
  And would I send yours to the grave
  Because, thanks to the chance that governs birth,
  I have the gift of expressing... what you perhaps feel?
